articles.title: Live K-pop show makes South Korea more real to former North Korean arts troupe singer
articles.excerpt: “I really am in the South now,” said Cho Mi-young - at her first K-pop show - 22 years after…
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean .
A white tiger entered the courtyard outside the National Museum in Seoul. He mugged for the camera and darted up the steps. At the top were the six members of BOYNEXTDOOR, wearing quasi-traditional outfits that mixed elements of hanbok with modern formal wear and a tinge of “bad boy” biker gear.
As they danced in unison and sang the opening lines of their hit single “Animal,” the crowd went wild.
Sitting in the audience was Cho Mi-young – born in Chongjin, North Korea – who arrived with her family in the South in 2004.
Mi-young can’t contain herself. “You’re so amazing!” she cries out, as the monitors show the young men dominating the courtyard with their precise dance moves.
Cho is in the audience at an episode of KBS Music Bank, a Friday night K-pop showcase program with all the latest acts. It has been the start of the K-pop weekend for most of its 28-year runtime. Surprisingly, it’s her first time ever seeing a live K-pop performance in person after 22 years in the South.
Tickets to studio tapings of KBS Music Bank are hard to come by. Fans either have to know someone, know someone who knows someone, or enter the ticket lottery. The episode she’s watching on Oct. 16 is special - it’s a live broadcast and the biggest boy bands, girl bands, and boy-girl bands are plying their craft on an outdoor stage on the grounds of the National Museum of Korea, which the show’s special intro vignette called the “beating heart of Korean culture.”
When the opening act was finished, the show’s hosts began introducing this week’s lineup, as Cho and the rest of the audience settled in. Many more K-pop groups and solo artists would take the stage in front of them on a night they would likely all remember forever.
“I’ve seen it a lot on TV, but today is the first time I’ve seen it with my own eyes,” Cho told Radio Free Asia. “Seeing such beautiful and handsome people dancing and singing right in front of me, moving like that, is absolutely mesmerizing.”
Cho is no stranger to music, or to the stage. In North Korea she had been a vocalist for a state-run provincial arts troupe. After settling in the South, Cho was a fixture in Seoul’s burgeoning musical theater scene and she toured as an accordion player. She later transitioned into broadcasting, at one point even co-hosting the RFA Korean webseries “ Northboy Northgirl .”
At present, she runs a content production company and maintains an active presence both online and in traditional media.
Cho Mi-young watches a live broadcast of KBS Music Bank at the National Museum of Korea in Seoul, Oct. 16, 2026.
(RFA) But today, she’s just a fangirl in a sea of other diehards, most of whom are screaming the names of the idols on stage.
Music in isolation
On the night of her first live K-pop concert, Cho reminisced about how she first encountered South Korean music in North Korea. At the time, she didn’t have access to what most would describe as K-pop today; instead she took in a lot of trot – a unique South Korean genre that mixes Western foxtrot dance rhythms with pentatonic minor scale melodies. Most young South Koreans consider trot to be music their grandparents like.
But after arriving in the South, she became a huge fan of South Korean love ballads, much slower than the catchiest K-pop numbers, but thicker in emotion. Music occupied much of her daily life in the South early on, as she scanned the radio for something new to listen to.
Today’s performances on the Music Bank stage were a far cry from her own back in North Korea. For one, everyone on stage just seems happy to be there, she said.
“When I performed in North Korea, I was always stiff,” she said. “When we were on stage, we performed with the mindset of conveying the Party’s voice, so I don’t think I ever had the thought that we were actually enjoying our own music.”
Several more musical acts came and went and then the undistorted electric guitar of indie rock band Jannabi’s Kim Do-hyung echoed through the air as vocalist Choi Jung-hoon sang the first few lyrics of “Thoughts on an Autumn Night.”
“Even on that distant shining star up there… love must be alive singing its song.”
The song struck a chord with Cho. Performed by just one singer and one guitarist it was a bit of a shift from the rest of the evening’s heavily choreographed bangers.
“The lyrical melody seems to have a bit of North Korean sensibility to it.”
She sat there, transfixed by Jannabi’s intimate, scaled down performance on the stage and quietly sang along.
“I really am in the South now”
When it was all over, Cho talked about her experience on the show, but it wasn’t only the dazzle of the K-pop acts that caught her eye. She was also amazed by the devoted fans, who sang along with every lyric from memory and chanted in pre-arranged cheers in unison. She thought back to how strange that seemed when she first arrived.
“I didn’t understand it in the past. But as I’ve lived here longer, I’ve come to understand the fans and their pre-prepared chants,” she said. “I think maybe next time, I might enjoy it even more if I learned those.”
The best performance of the evening, according to Cho, was by a co-ed group called AllDay Project. She thought they looked cool in their all-black outfits, some in furs, others in biker leather – almost like warriors.
But as an artist, Cho’s thoughts naturally turned to the massive effort that must have gone on behind the scenes. The meticulous choreography alone must take many months of practice, she said.
She recalled how she herself had put in a lot of effort as a singer back in North Korea.
“Even in North Korea, artists are trained very strictly in a Spartan manner,” she said. “In terms of the sheer volume of training, it might be difficult to see a significant difference between the North and South.”
But she noted that the payoff in the South is individual success, unlike the North, where it would merely advance the goals of the state.
She said the whole evening was surreal. Back when she was in North Korea, she could maybe catch glimpses of what the music scene in the South was like, but she could never actually see it. Now she finally has seen it in person, “it sinks in that I really am in the South now.”
Cho said that she thinks any North Korean escapee would probably feel the same way.
“The emotion felt in the live setting is completely different from listening to a recording,” she said. “I think many escapees would finally feel they truly have arrived in South Korea when they go to the venue, see the singer in person, and listen to the songs live.”
Edited by Yi Yongin in Korean and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: China closes 3 Tibetan schools in 3 months; threatens language, cultural preservation
articles.excerpt: Shutting schools in Golog region, Qinghai province, comes three months after "ethnic unity law" enacted on July 1.
articles.fullText:
Chinese authorities have shut down three Tibetan schools in the Golog region of Qinghai province in recent months, leaving the fate of students and teachers unclear, according to sources inside Tibet.
The closures of Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School, Jasag Village Primary School and Golog Tadra Orphan School have raised concerns among Tibetans about the future of education that incorporates their language, cultural traditions and community life.
Tibetan sources who spoke to Radio Free Asia linked the closures to the Chinese government’s education policies and its promotion of the Ethnic Unity and Progress Law , which took effect on July 1, 2026. They said the shutdowns could further limit opportunities for Tibetan children to learn their mother tongue and cultural traditions.
The Chinese government has cited the high altitude of Golog and shortages of teachers and educational resources as reasons for establishing schools outside the region, saying the move would improve education. It remains unclear where students from the three closed schools will continue their studies.
Education department declines to comment
RFA contacted the education department of the Golog Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture by phone to seek details about the closures.
“We don’t know the details,” the person told RFA, saying the initial work had been carried out by the Machen County administration and that the county’s education department was responsible for the matter.
RFA also contacted the Machen County Education Department, which said it had “no authority to respond.”
Unclear future for students
Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School in Ragya Township, Machen County, was closed on Aug. 28, according to a source in Tibet who spoke to RFA on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
The school had about 450 students and 60 teachers at the time of its closure, the source said. The current situation of the students remains unclear.
Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School in an undated photo.
(Citizen photo) The source said the school had been made a government-affiliated institution, with its curriculum following the Chinese government’s education system while retaining some Tibetan-language instruction.
“Currently, the schools in the Golog region are conducting a strong patriotic reeducation campaign,” the source said, adding that Tibetans were afraid to share information because of government restrictions.
Jasag Village Primary School, which was established in 1995 with funds raised by local nomadic families and renamed Ragya Township Residential School No. 2 in 2008, was shut down in September, according to information obtained by RFA. Another source in Tibet told RFA that the situation of its students and teachers remained unclear.
“The Golog Education Department has put considerable pressure on the school’s teachers and shut down the school without providing any clear explanation,” the source said.
Golog Tadra Orphanage School was ordered to close this month, according to information obtained by RFA. Founded in 2005, it provided education and support to Tibetan orphans and disadvantaged children for two decades.
At an event marking the school’s 20th anniversary in 2025, principal Thupten Nyima of the Golog Tadra Orphan School, which provides K-12 education, said it was training more than 1,000 students. Some graduates had gone on to work in government positions and as teachers, he said.
Nyima addressed students and teachers in a recent video posted to social media, saying, “Don’t be sad, students and teachers. If we are bound by karma and fate, all the teachers and students gathered here will sing a song of joy together.”
It is unclear if Nyima’s remarks were made around the time the school was ordered to close.
Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School in an undated photo.
(Citizen photo) Critics warn of cultural impact
Dr. Gyal Lo, a Tibetan educational sociologist, said the closures marked a significant change in the Chinese government’s education policy in Tibet.
“The Chinese government sees schools where Tibetans can organize themselves to learn and teach their own culture as a thorn in its side. That is why these schools are being abolished,” he told RFA.
“After Xi Jinping visited Qinghai, the school established by Jigme Gyaltsen was closed , and a new secondary school was built in the eastern part of Ziling,” he said.
Gyal Lo said the closures could distance children from Tibetan traditions and customs practiced in their communities and place them in state-run boarding schools where Chinese is the language of instruction.
“The first impact of the Chinese government’s school closures is that children are distanced from the Tibetan traditions and customs practiced in their homeland. Secondly, when these children enter state-run boarding schools, the entire curriculum is taught in Chinese and is under the government’s control,” he said.
He argued that the policies could affect the transmission of Tibetan identity across generations.
“The aim is to turn the entire Tibetan people into Chinese. This is not limited to a small area; it is a plan with far-reaching consequences,” Gyal Lo told RFA. “The ultimate goal is to turn the younger generation of Tibetans into Chinese through different methods and policies implemented in different regions.”
He also emphasized the role of families in preserving the Tibetan language.
“According to language education theory, a language cannot be passed on to the next generation without being taught within the family. The foundation for preserving the mother tongue and passing it on to the next generation must be laid at home,” he said.
Tenzin Lekshey, spokesperson for the Central Tibetan Administration in Dharamsala, India, said Tibetan schools and monasteries played an important role in preserving the community’s language, culture, traditions and identity.
“The Chinese government is doing all this out of fear. Tibetan schools and monasteries established inside Tibet aim to preserve and protect the rich Tibetan language, culture, traditions and identity. But the Chinese government views these institutions as a hindrance rather than a benefit,” he told RFA.
Ragya Geshe Lobsang Palden, a former political prisoner, said the new ethnic unity law had coincided with the closure of several Tibetan schools, some of which had already been brought under government control.
“These schools could not be shut down before because it was not legally appropriate to do so. Now, with the new Ethnic Unity Law in effect since July, many schools have been closing down,” he told RFA.
“However, many of these schools had already been converted into government-affiliated schools several years ago,” he added.
Dawa Tashi, a researcher at the Tibetan Centre for Human Rights and Democracy in Dharamsala, also linked the closures to the new law, saying it formalized policies that threatened Tibetan cultural and linguistic identity.
A former Tibetan political prisoner who visited Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School in 2006 said many of its graduates had gone on to serve their communities. The source requested anonymity for security reasons.
“I remember speaking with a teacher at the school in 2006 who told me that several teachers had been summoned by Chinese authorities. The teacher anticipated that the school might eventually be closed,” the source told RFA.
New government boarding schools
The closures come amid a broader restructuring of education in Golog, where authorities have promoted Chinese-language education and campaigns emphasizing national unity.
On Sept. 1, 2026 the Golog Education Department officially opened the newly established Golog Tsoshar Middle School in eastern Qinghai. According to Chinese state media, the school enrolled 1,200 students, including 1,090 Tibetans, many from farming and nomadic families.
Authorities have described the relocation of students from Golog to the lower-lying Tsoshar area as part of an effort to expand residential education in the highlands. It remains unclear whether students from Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School were transferred to the new institution.
Golog Ziling (Xining) Middle School, a state-run boarding school in Xining, was also opened on Sept. 1, 2019. According to official figures for 2024, it had 800 students, including 778 Tibetans, all from Golog. The school’s official introduction identifies fostering a shared sense of community among the Chinese nation as a central goal of its education.
In September 2026, the Golog prefecture government also launched a public language promotion week encouraging students to learn and use standard Chinese and emphasizing unity among the Chinese people.
Earlier school closures
The latest shutdowns follow several other closures of Tibetan educational institutions in Golog in recent years.
In July 2024, authorities closed Gangjong Sherig Norling School in Machen County after 30 years of operation. Founded by Jigme Gyaltsen in 1994, the institution had about 1,400 students and 58 teachers and staff.
The vocational school combined modern education with instruction in Tibetan language, culture, philosophy and religion. Reports in April 2025 indicated that authorities had permitted it to reopen as a vocational institution, although its curriculum was expected to change.
Dorjeten National Vocational School in Chikdril County (in Golog) was shut down on Dec. 12, 2025, affecting more than 1,300 students, according to reports. Hungkar Dorje Vocational Secondary School in Golog was also closed on June 24, 2026.
The latest closures have raised further questions about the future of Tibetan-language education in the region and whether students from the affected schools will continue to have opportunities to learn their language and cultural traditions.
Background: The three schools
Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School
Founded in 2005 by Tibetan educator Jigme Gyaltsen in Ragya Township, the school was established to provide education for girls, including those from nomadic communities. When it officially opened on Oct. 15, 2005, it had 203 students and 15 teachers. Its curriculum included Tibetan, Chinese and English, as well as mathematics, science, culture and sports.
Gyaltsen described his educational philosophy as follows: “The education of girls is the education of mothers, and the education of mothers is the foundation of human education.”
Jasag Village Primary School
Established in 1995 with funds raised by local nomadic families through the former Jasag Village Committee, the school served children from the surrounding community. It was renamed Ragya Township Residential School No. 2 in 2008 and closed in September 2026.
Golog Tadra Orphan School
Founded in 2005 by the late Dr. Tawo Lobsang Palden and his wife, Choenyi Lhamo, the school provided education, accommodation, food, clothing and health care to Tibetan orphans and disadvantaged children. Over two decades, it served thousands of children. Lhamo now lives in Germany.
Translated by Tenzin Dickyi and edited by Tawang for RFA Tibetan

articles.title: CE congratulates HK athletes
articles.excerpt: Chief Executive John Lee today congratulated Hong Kong, China athletes on their achievements at the 5th Asian Para Games, commending…
articles.fullText:
Chief Executive John Lee today congratulated Hong Kong, China athletes on their achievements at the 5th Asian Para Games, commending their outstanding performance and noble sportsmanship.

Mr Lee said the Hong Kong, China delegation delivered an excellent performance at this year's Asian Para Games, winning a total of 41 medals, comprising 3 gold, 14 silver and 24 bronze medals, and achieving Hong Kong's best-ever result in boccia with a total of 2 gold, 3 silver, and 3 bronze medals.

He said these heartening achievements write a splendid chapter in the development of para sports in Hong Kong.

"Hong Kong, China athletes gave their utmost in the competition, demonstrating superb skills and indomitable determination. Their achievements have not only brought honour to Hong Kong, but also inspired the community with their perseverance and never-give-up sportsmanship. Their outstanding performance has earned the admiration and pride of the entire Hong Kong community.”

Mr Lee stressed that the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government has always attached great importance to sports development for persons with disabilities, helping them to realise their potential and pursue their dreams. Through the Hong Kong Sports Institute, the Government provides full-time high-level training for elite athletes with disabilities. This allows them to receive professional coaching, with access to barrier-free world-class training venues and equipment, and comprehensive support in sports science and sports medicine, enabling them to represent Hong Kong, China in competitions in the Mainland and abroad.

The Chief Executive added that the Government last year raised the level of direct financial support for elite athletes with disabilities across the board, and for the first time introduced a Senior Squad funding tier. This further enhances the training pathway.

Mr Lee said Hong Kong's outstanding performance at this year's Asian Para Games demonstrates that the Government's policy direction is the right one.

"I would like to thank all the athletes, coaches, medical teams and support personnel for their tireless efforts and dedication. The Government will continue to work closely with the China Hong Kong Paralympic Committee, the Hong Kong Sports Institute and various national sports associations to devote resources to nurturing talent, helping more athletes with disabilities unleash their potential, surpass themselves and achieve new levels in future international competitions."

articles.title: Counter-terrorism exhibition opens
articles.excerpt: The Inter-departmental Counter Terrorism Unit (ICTU) is staging an educational counter-terrorism exhibition in the Hong Kong Museum of History. Co-organised…
articles.fullText:
The Inter-departmental Counter Terrorism Unit (ICTU) is staging an educational counter-terrorism exhibition in the Hong Kong Museum of History.

Co-organised by the National Security Department of the Hong Kong Police Force and co-ordinated by the Security Bureau, the exhibition aims to enhance public awareness of counter-terrorism (CT) and strengthen public response capabilities through multimedia displays and interactive experiences.

Addressing today's opening ceremony, Secretary for Security Tang Ping-keung emphasised that terrorism knows no borders. He said Hong Kong must therefore remain vigilant and be prepared for potential threats, while continuing to strengthen the city’s CT capabilities in the areas of prevention, preparedness, response and recovery.

Mr Tang outlined that the exhibition aims to deepen public understanding of terrorism, the global CT landscape, and Hong Kong's strategies. It also seeks to encourage members of the public to stay alert, embrace the message that “greater vigilance means lower risk”, and work together to safeguard Hong Kong’s security.

The exhibition, located in the main lobby of the museum, will run until March 1 next year. Together with the National Security Exhibition Gallery on the second floor, it offers a complementary and synergistic exhibition experience.

Featuring diverse and vibrant content across multiple zones, the exhibition showcases the global and local CT landscape; Hong Kong’s strategies, including the Government's Three-tier Prevention Framework for CT, and the relevant legal framework; as well as the CT roles of the ICTU and other government departments.

It also has interactive elements such as the “Spot and Report” and “Run, Hide, Report” games, together with an authentic wartime bomb weighing over 1,000 pounds. Dismantled in 2014, it has been provided for display by the Police Explosive Ordnance Disposal Bureau.

The exhibition enables visitors to gain CT and emergency preparedness knowledge through immersive and interactive experiences, thereby enhancing public awareness of terrorism prevention.

In addition, "Safe Community Plus+”, jointly organised by the ICTU and the Hong Kong Federation of Youth Groups for a third time, also officially launched following the opening ceremony. It will visit various schools and community venues over the next six months, using a variety of interactive mini-games to help students and the public to learn about security awareness and emergency response in an engaging manner.

articles.title: Public alerted to fake messages
articles.excerpt: The Department of Health today alerted the public to suspicious emails and SMS messages sent by its HIV Testing Service…
articles.fullText:
The Department of Health today alerted the public to suspicious emails and SMS messages sent by its HIV Testing Service website.

The department said the email account for the website is suspected of having been misused, with emails and text messages being sent to the public wrongly indicating that recipients were exposed to Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), and should seek medical advice and get tested as soon as possible.

The department is conducting a thorough investigation into the incident. It said it has not yet found any evidence of data loss or leakage.

Emphasising that the emails and SMS messages were wrongly sent, the department highlighted that it does not notify individuals in this manner. It advised members of the public who receive suspicious emails or SMS messages not to click on any links contained in them or provide personal information. Anyone who has provided personal information to suspicious individuals or suspects that they have been scammed should contact the Police Force.

The department said it immediately conducted a comprehensive inspection of its network system with the outsourced service provider upon discovering the issue last night and also reported it to the force and notified the Digital Policy Office.

The HIV Testing Service website is suspended from today until cybersecurity experts have conducted a comprehensive investigation and review to confirm that there are no security risks. Members of the public can still call the Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome Hotline on 2780 2211 to arrange a free, anonymous and confidential HIV antibody test while the website is suspended.

The Government stressed that it attaches great importance to cybersecurity. The department conducts regular information security risk assessments, and will continue to review and enhance existing measures to keep abreast of the times in order to safeguard network and system security.

articles.title: China’s sanctions on Taiwan allies project its power, but with limited effect
articles.excerpt: Beijing sent a message by sanctioning officials from Paraguay and Belize, but both remain loyal to Taipei.
articles.fullText:
China’s sanctions against foreign officials over their ties with Taiwan help Beijing project power and warn other governments, even as their financial impact and success in curbing engagement remain limited, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
Beijing imposed sanctions on Oct. 12 against Paraguay’s information and communication technologies minister, Gustavo Villate, and Belize’s foreign minister, Francis Fonseca. Both countries maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan rather than China.
China claims Taiwan is an integral part of its territory and considers it a rogue province. Beijing has sought to persuade governments to switch recognition from Taiwan to China, reducing Taiwan’s network of embassies and official government-to-government relationships.
The Chinese government has described the sanctions as a “warning and deterrence.”
The national flags of Paraguay and Taiwan flutter outside the building housing Taiwan's embassy, in Asuncion, Paraguay, Feb. 25, 2026.
(Cesar Olmedo/Reuters) When China sanctions individuals they don’t quite have the same effect as U.S. or European sanctions, Ed Moon, an independent cross-Strait analyst and founder of intelligence site Strait Signal, told RFA.
“Chinese sanctions are unlikely to have significant impacts on people without major interests in the Chinese banking system, shareholdings or business interests,” he said.
But the penalties serve a purpose beyond imposing financial losses, said Moon. They signal to observers in China and abroad that Beijing can enforce restrictions when it believes its interests have been harmed, and can serve as a warning to countries closely connected to the Chinese economy about dealings with sanctioned individuals.
While sanctions could discourage engagement with Taiwan, there is little evidence that the strategy is causing isolation for Taipei, William Yang, a Northeast Asia analyst at the Belgium-based International Crisis Group, told RFA.
“We haven’t really seen a substantial level of retreat in terms of foreign parliamentarians’ trips to Taiwan or foreign governments’ cooperation with Taiwan,” Yang said.
The assessments point to a distinction between two types of sanctions: those that impose measurable costs and those whose principal effect is to publicize Beijing’s opposition to Taiwan’s international relationships.
Isolating Taiwan
Only 12 countries retain formal diplomatic relations with Taipei. Taiwan also maintains extensive unofficial relationships with countries that recognize Beijing. Those ties include trade, investment and parliamentary exchanges, explaining why China’s penalties have targeted politicians beyond Taiwan’s formal diplomatic allies.
Yang said Beijing’s campaign is meant to show Taiwan’s government and people that it has the power to restrict international engagement with Taipei, while simultaneously showing foreign governments that there will be consequences for treating Taiwan as a sovereign state.
He added Beijing believes its economic influence gives it leverage to intimidate politicians and governments considering closer engagement with Taipei.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said during an Oct. 12 press briefing that the ministers from Paraguay and Belize were sanctioned for supporting Taiwan independence through their contacts with Taipei and spreading false allegations about Chinese cyberattacks.
Belize's Prime Minister Johnny Briceno, left, meets with Taiwan's Vice President Lai Ching-te in Honduras, Jan. 27, 2022.
(Taiwan Presidential Office/AP) The next day, Taiwan’s Premier Cho Jung-tai said that Beijing had no right to interfere in Taiwan’s internal affairs or influence its foreign relations. He said Taiwan would continue working with its allies and other democratic governments to defend freedom and democracy and maintain regional peace and security.
Paraguay and Belize also rejected the sanctions. Paraguay’s Foreign Ministry reaffirmed its support for Taiwan, while Belize said the penalties would not alter its foreign policy and defended its relationship with Taipei as a sovereign decision.
Their cooperation involves more than diplomatic recognition. Paraguayan President Santiago Peña visited Taiwan in May, signing agreements covering cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and computing investment, among other areas. Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung visited Belize in September to deepen bilateral ties.
Do Chinese sanctions work?
Previous cases of Chinese sanctions show the difficulty of turning personal penalties into lasting restrictions on engagement.
In June, China confirmed entry restrictions against New Zealand lawmakers following their visit to Taiwan. Beijing said their trip interfered in China’s internal affairs.
From right to left, Taiwan's Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim, speaking with New Zealand lawmakers Maureen Pugh, Duncan Webb, Laura McClure and David Wilson at the Presidential Office in Taipei, May 7, 2026.
(Presidential Office of Taiwan/AFP) In August 2022, China sanctioned Lithuania’s deputy transport minister, Agnė Vaiciukevičiūtė, after she visited Taiwan. Beijing also suspended exchanges with Vilnius’ transport ministry and paused certain international transportation agreements between the two countries.
That action formed part of a wider dispute after Lithuania allowed a Taiwanese representative office to open in the country in 2021. China downgraded diplomatic relations over the decision.
Cooperation with Taiwan nevertheless continued. Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry reported discussions in April 2026 on strengthening economic and technological ties.
The broader outcome is more complicated. Lithuania’s prime minister described the original representative-office decision as a mistake in February as the country sought to repair relations with Beijing.
Because the dispute involved broader diplomatic and economic pressure, analysts say it is difficult to isolate the impact of sanctions against a single official.
Moon said the same difficulty applied to Paraguay and Belize – Beijing has used various public and private forms of pressure for years, so any subsequent policy change could not automatically be attributed to the latest sanctions.
He said changes in diplomatic language, visits and, at the most dramatic end, diplomatic recognition would provide indicators of whether the relationships were shifting.
Past sanctions have also produced backlash.
In March 2021, Beijing sanctioned European lawmakers and institutions in retaliation for European Union sanctions over human rights abuses in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region. Although the dispute concerned human rights rather than Taiwan, it similarly targeted individual politicians and their institutions.
The European Parliament responded by freezing consideration of an EU-China investment agreement while the Chinese sanctions remained in place. Beijing lifted the sanctions affecting the EU Parliament’s members and committees in 2025.
Moon said sanctions could carry greater economic weight when directed at people or companies with business interests in China, including in Taiwan.
In a separate action on Oct. 14, Beijing announced restrictions against VWAY, a company linked to the father of Taiwanese legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen.
Pedestrians walk past a giant campaign billboard featuring the Democratic Progressive Party's Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen in Taipei on Oct. 15, 2026.
(I-Hwa Cheng/AFP) China’s Taiwan Affairs Office accused Shen’s father of using VWAY to continue trading with Chinese firms after sanctions were placed on another of his businesses.
Moon cautioned that Taiwan-related business sanctions were not directly comparable with penalties against foreign governments’ officials, given Beijing’s position that Taiwan is part of China.
Yang said the sanctions’ limited results so far did not rule out a stronger deterrent effect in the future. Responses by Taiwan’s remaining diplomatic allies, including whether they protested collectively or moved toward recognizing Beijing, would be important to watch, he said.
“So far it seems like at least the government of Paraguay and Belize are holding their lines,” said Yang.
Beijing could still regard the publicity itself as a result, reinforcing its claims over Taiwan and demonstrating that engagement with Taipei carried consequences, Moon said.
“But I think for Beijing the mere fact it has created a news cycle out of the sanctions will mean it has achieved the desired effect of reinforcing its claims over Taiwan and showing there are consequences, however limited, to siding with Taipei.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.fullText:
This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Are we there yet? A reality check on six big tech promises

Some seemingly impossible feats are too good to give up on. Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Absolutely. Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Yes, please. Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but how close are we, really?

In the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review , we ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years, or even decades. From exercise in a pill to nuclear-powered spaceships, we asked experts what’s holding them back and how far they’ve come.

Check out our stories on how they all stacked up .

Over the coming days, we’ll unpack each of the six technologies in The Download. So stay tuned!

In the biotech world, you can’t see everything

—Jessica Hamzelou

Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything , the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.

Like many others, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.

The film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. This is why it left me questioning how we cover science .

This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.

Help choose our next Roundtables topic

Our subscriber-only Roundtables bring you into conversation with MIT Technology Review editors and reporters. Now, we want your help choosing our next topic: how to keep your mind going for longer, or what it would take to put a city on the moon. Which do you most want to hear about?

Vote for your preferred topic by Monday at 12 p.m. ET .

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Palmer Luckey’s new startup plans to genetically enhance military dogs
Warhound says the dogs will detect explosives and protect troops. ( Wired $)
+ It’s raised $200 million from investors, including Sequoia. ( TechCrunch )
+ Colossal Biosciences will help clone and gene-edit the dogs. ( Bloomberg $)
+ The Pentagon wants an AI-powered lie detector. ( MIT Technology Review )

2 Donald Trump says Elon Musk has restored Ukraine’s Starlink access
But Zelensky says Starlink speeds remained capped. ( Reuters $)
+ Trump reportedly asked Musk to lift the speed limits. ( WSJ $)

3 The newly disclosed PHP flaw is yet to yield successful attacks
Experts say the vulnerabilities are harder to exploit than expected. ( NBC News )
+ Officials urged patches after the flaws forced websites offline worldwide . ( BBC )
+ But publicly disclosed fixes can help hackers. ( The Economist $)

4 Moderna and Merck say their mRNA cancer vaccine cut death by 42%
The vaccine reduced melanoma patients’ risk of recurrence. ( Ars Technica )
+ Federal health agencies are abandoning mRNA. ( MIT Technology Review )

5 A powerful new gene editor has reached its first human patient
The prime editing technique rewrites DNA in liver cells. ( Nature )
+ Companies are planning gene-edited babies. ( MIT Technology Review )

6 Google will pay customers to free up power for data centers
Its virtual power plant will reward people for adjusting energy usage. ( NYT $)
+ It’s also illegally felled 250,000 trees in Finland for a data center. ( Guardian )

7 Dutch spies reportedly hacked Jared Kushner’s iPhone
The report alleges financial links to foreign officials. ( Vanity Fair $)

8 Fossil fuels may have stopped the next ice age
Modern warming reversed 2,000 years of ice growth. ( Wired $)

9 Scientists have recreated solar flares to explain the corona’s mystery
They hope to explain why it’s so hot. ( New Scientist $)

10 A road trip with America’s cheapest EV shows charging is much improved
Fast chargers kept the journey manageable despite sparse coverage. ( WSJ $)
+ And bigger EVs aren’t always better. ( MIT Technology Review )

Quote of the day

“If anything happens to this guy, that’s just it. Everyone is screwed.”

—Software developer Ian Landsman says on X that volunteer Ondřej Surý’s work on patching PHP vulnerabilities makes him an unsung hero of the entire internet.

One more thing

STUART BRADFORD

How sounds can turn us on to the wonders of the universe

For decades, astronomy has relied on visual information to make sense of the cosmos: images, charts, and graphs. Now, some researchers are trying something different: listening to the universe.

Using sonification, the process of turning information into sound, they’re helping blind and visually impaired researchers explore the cosmos—and even uncover patterns that might otherwise go unnoticed. The approach is spreading beyond astronomy into fields like climate science, navigation, and education.

Discover how sound could make science more accessible—and even more revealing .

—Corey S. Powell

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ A team of domino experts broke a Guinness World Record with a 29,193-piece 3D pyramid.
+ Scientists suspect that pigeons sense Earth’s magnetic fields using specialized immune cells in their livers .
+ See inside cells like never before with these vivid microscopic images from the Nikon Small World competitions.

articles.title: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
articles.excerpt: Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything , the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced…
articles.fullText:
Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything , the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.

I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood , and the Hulu series The Dropout , starring Amanda Seyfried.

Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything .

In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood.

Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old.

Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead. MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015 .

Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong.

In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023.

It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film.

As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer , there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people. And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out. Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind. Will anyone believe her?

I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence. And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator. You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind. At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat. Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie?

But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune ’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT ’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015. Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022 .

I didn’t cover Theranos in the 2010s. If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all?

One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data. Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification. Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process. You should be able to trust published scientific papers.

Except that sometimes you can’t.

Scientists aren’t perfect. Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance. Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis. Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always. There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence. Many papers ultimately end up with corrections. Some are withdrawn— 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 .

At any rate, there’s been a shift to sharing research in other ways. Today, many scientists opt to publish their work at preprint servers like arXiv, medRxiv, and bioRxiv before they submit them to established journals. Those outlets bypass peer review. So do company press releases, social media posts, and many conference presentations. And I get a lot of my stories from conversations and interviews.

I’ll admit I’ve looked at a scientific finding and thought: A scientist has just said they’ve done that. How can I be sure they really have?

I like to think that I hold myself to high journalistic standards here, as does everyone at MIT Technology Review . I would never publish a story about some new scientific development without doing my own form of peer review, and asking scientists—ideally people I know and trust—what they think of a new claim.

But the film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. While most scientists are, I hope, pretty honest, and Holmes is certainly an outlier, we should all continue to interrogate the claims being fed to us. If you’ve seen the film, let me know what you think!

This article first appeared in The Checkup,  MIT Technology Review’s  weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first,  sign up here .

articles.title: Designing an AI serving harness built to last
articles.excerpt: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you…
articles.fullText:
The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it.

That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?”

Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management , scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability.

For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it.

Start with the workload, not the model

There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture. There is only the right solution for the business problem.

A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight. An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures.

The workload defines the constraints. The constraints should determine the architecture.

That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments. During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion. Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic.

A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application’s latency requirements. Not every workload needs a Ferrari. Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn’t.

The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload. That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern. It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn’t worth the cost.

Engineer the system, not the model

Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another. Serving architecture influences memory utilization. Memory management affects concurrency. Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency.

Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value. This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance.

GPU memory is a good example. During inference, the model’s weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length. As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available. Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive.

The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize . Identify the dominant constraint. Address it. Measure the result. Then determine if another bottleneck emerged. Repeat.

Don’t think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn’t to collect them all. The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application’s business requirements.

For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question. Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value.

Build for change, not today’s benchmark

Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today’s leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s. Models will improve. Hardware will evolve. New optimization techniques will emerge. The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances.

That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy.

Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs. A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset.

EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series. It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable.

Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models. Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes.

The model provides the intelligence. The harness determines whether the enterprise can deliver outcomes reliably, economically, and at scale.

articles.title: ‘I hope that she will be free before long’ Aung San Suu Kyi’s son Kim Aris says
articles.excerpt: Kim Aris talks to RFA after his first direct contact in 5 years with his mother, under house arrest in…
articles.fullText:
Myanmar’s military-backed government announced on Thursday that former leader Aung San Suu Kyi – currently under house arrest – was allowed to talk for 20 minutes to her son Kim Aris at 2:30 p.m. via a call placed to the Myanmar embassy in London, where Aris resides.
He speaks in an exclusive interview with Radio Free Asia.
Radio Free Asia: After more than five years without direct contact, how did you get the opportunity to speak with your mother and how did the Myanmar Embassy in London reach out to you? How was the call arranged?
Kim Aris: I was informed through the British Foreign Office here that the call may take place. This was last week. And then earlier this week, they confirmed that it would take place, and they accompanied me to the Burmese Embassy this morning.
RFA: During your conversation, did Daw Aung San Suu Kyi mention anything about her health or her daily life?
Kim Aris: Well, she was more concerned about my health and the rest of the family than anything else. But obviously, I asked after her health and how things were, where she is. She wasn’t able to reveal too much, but I know that she’s been held in some residence, I believe in Naypyidaw, and she sounds healthy. But at the same time, I know that she is in some pain because her hand is not very well; she has tendonitis. So at times, the pain is quite extreme, and I think she is even unable to use that hand at times. Nothing too clear. I know that she’s getting a regular six-monthly checkup, but I know that will be a military doctor, so it’s not like having her own personal doctor.
RFA: Do you know whether she has any access to news from the outside world?
Kim Aris: I don’t think she does. As far as I’m aware, she has no radio or television and doesn’t get any newspapers or anything like that. We know that the conversation will have been monitored and recorded, so we can’t talk about anything sensitive. Besides which, there was a lot to talk about just talking about what’s happened in the family over the last five years. So that’s what we talked about.
RFA: During these recent developments , do you believe there could be a political breakthrough on the horizon?
Kim Aris: I sincerely hope so. I think everybody is tired of the fighting now, and people are starting to think that they need to start talking to each other. But I think the first thing that needs to happen before anybody will start talking is the political prisoners, including may may (Burmese expression for “mom”), need to be freed.
RFA: Some observers believe the Myanmar authorities may be looking for a way out of Myanmar’s ongoing political crisis. What is your take on this?
Kim Aris: Well, it’s very clear the military have been trying to be more appealing to the international community, especially following their elections at the end of last year and the beginning of this year. So they are doing whatever they can to try and get people to work with them again. But people need to remember that the military haven’t actually abided by any of what they have said they will have done over the last five years. They have not met the five-point consensus, and yet people are starting to re-engage with them without having seen any evidence of actual progress.
RFA: The Myanmar military authorities have recently been releasing more information about Daw Aung San Suu Kyi. Do you see this as a reason for optimism? What do you think the Myanmar military’s move might be?
Kim Aris: I always have hope, and I do hope that this will result in actual progress and that she will be free before long. And even before she’s free, I want more regular contact with her, and I want to know that she’s receiving external medical treatment.
RFA: Did they promise you could speak with Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, your mother, regularly?
Kim Aris: No, I haven’t heard anything more on that yet.
RFA: You made it very clear that your mother should never be used as a bargaining chip for diplomatic recognition, sanctions relief, or political advantage. You also urged the UK government and others not to trade humanitarian rights for political legitimacy. And now, one of our RFA audience members raised a difficult question. They asked if negotiation and compromise may be necessary to secure your mother Daw Aung San Suu Kyi’s release. How would you respond to that?
Kim Aris: Well, I realize there are people who have been calling for my mother’s release all the time for the last five years, and without their support, I wouldn’t even have gotten this far. And people do have to negotiate—that’s very clear. At the same time, they should not be legitimizing the military by open discussions like this and welcoming Min Aung Hlaing to their country without actually having secured progress.
RFA: After hearing your mother’s voice for the first time in more than five years, what message would you like to share with the Myanmar people or international community?
Kim Aris: Well, I would say she is sounding well and strong still, but at 81 years old and with ongoing health concerns, and we still don’t know what conditions she’s really been kept under, I’d ask for everybody to continue to fight for her freedom. Burma needs to come forwards, and may may is part of that process still. People need to talk to one another, and one of the few people who is actually able to get people to talk to one another is may may . So please, do not stop fighting for her freedom. Fighting for her freedom is also fighting for the freedom of Burma.
Edited by Charlie Dharapak.

A scalable AI system requires a strong foundation. Data, engineering, platforms, operating models, and governance must converge to work as one. This session from MIT Technology Review’s EmTech Future conference explores what it takes to build that foundation in a highly regulated environment and how a responsible, trustworthy implementation can turn emerging capabilities, including agentic systems, into lasting value for investors.

About the speaker

Jing Wang, Principal, Center for AI and Insights, Vanguard

Jing Wang leads Vanguard’s Center for AI & Insights (CAI), advancing the firm’s AI, machine learning, generative AI, and behavioral science capabilities. Her team drives enterprise-wide innovation, research, and delivery, enabling Vanguard to translate emerging technologies into trusted solutions that enhance client experiences, improve investor outcomes, and create measurable business value.

Before her current position, Jing served in a range of leadership roles across Vanguard’s Financial Services, Workplace Solutions, International, and Corporate Services divisions. Throughout her tenure, she has led teams and enterprise initiatives that advanced strategic priorities, strengthened client outcomes, and drove business performance across the firm.

She joined Vanguard in 2009 after several years as a Principal at the Boston Consulting Group. Jing earned a B.S. in Physics from the University of Science and Technology of China, a Ph.D. from the University of Pennsylvania, and an M.B.A. in Finance and Marketing from the Wharton School of Business at the University of Pennsylvania. Jing holds Series 7, 24, and 65 licenses.

articles.title: Aung San Suu Kyi phone call is ‘political calculation’ by military-backed government
articles.excerpt: Advocates demand full release of Myanmar's former leader after her first contact with family in 5 years.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Burmese
Updated 5:05 PM ET
Allowing Myanmar’s detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi to speak on the phone with her son for the first time in five years is not enough – the military government must immediately release her and all other political prisoners, a human rights advocate told Radio Free Asia Thursday.
The country’s military-backed government announced that the former leader – currently under house arrest – was allowed to talk for 20 minutes to her son Kim Aris at 2:30 p.m. via a call placed to the Myanmar embassy in London, where Aris resides.
The chance to talk to her son came just days after the military released images of her receiving a letter and some books sent by Britain’s King Charles III.
In this image released by the Myanmar government, Aung San Suu Kyi's son, Kim Aris, at the Myanmar embassy in London talks on the phone with his mother, in Naypyidaw, Myanmar, Oct. 22, 2026.
(Myanmar Presidential Spokesman via Reuters) While the phone call was a joyous occasion for mother and son, much more must be done to bring peace to Myanmar, Aung Myo Kyaw, an official with the Thailand-based Assistance Association for Political Prisoners (AAPP), told RFA.
“Aung San Suu Kyi is not only a mother to Kim, but also a mother to the country,” said Aung Myo Kyaw. “What the citizens of the country need is the release of all political prisoners, including Aung San Suu Kyi.”
He said that the gradual easing of restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi is a political calculation by the military government, which he said was failing in all aspects.
At a time when the military continues to airstrike populated areas of the country, simply allowing her to talk to her son in the U.K. will not bring peace, he said.
“FREE HER. FREE THEM ALL”
In an interview with Radio Free Asia after speaking with his mother, Kim Aris said that it’s clear that the Myanmar military-backed government have been trying to “be more appealing to the international community.”
“But people need to remember that the military haven’t actually abided by any of what they have said they will have done over the last five years,” Aris told RFA. “They have not met the five-point consensus, and yet people are starting to re-engage with them without having seen any evidence of actual progress.”
In a Facebook post, Aris said that he was glad to finally hear his mother’s voice again and thanked supporters for continuing to advocate for her freedom.
But he reiterated that she is still “unjustly detained.”
“One conversation is not regular family access. Family access is not freedom,” he said. “My mother must never be used as a hostage or bargaining chip for diplomatic recognition, sanctions relief or political advantage.”
He called on governments that engage with Myanmar’s military authorities to not legitimize them in exchange for humanitarian rights.
“My mother and all political prisoners must be released immediately and unconditionally. Freedom is not negotiable. Accountability Before Legitimacy. FREE HER. FREE THEM ALL,” he wrote.

Aung San Suu Kyi has been detained since the 2021 military coup that ousted her and the rest of the country’s democratically elected government from power. She was sentenced to 18 years for a broad range of crimes that include corruption and election fraud, though she maintains that she is innocent.
For the duration of her detention, her exact location has not been easy to ascertain, and in April the military government moved her into house arrest . Until the brief phone call with her son Thursday, she had had almost no contact with the outside.
Radio Free Asia attempted to contact a spokesman for the military government to discuss more details about the phone call between Aung San Suu Kyi and Kim Aris, but there was no response.
Updates with Kim Aris comment from RFA interview.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: FS visits Beijing
articles.excerpt: Financial Secretary Paul Chan today visited central ministries in Beijing and witnessed the signing of two Memoranda of Understanding on…
articles.fullText:
Financial Secretary Paul Chan today visited central ministries in Beijing and witnessed the signing of two Memoranda of Understanding on deepening economic and trade co-operations between the Mainland and Hong Kong.

In the morning, Mr Chan called on the China Securities Regulatory Commission and met its Chairman Wu Qing. They exchanged views in detail on strengthening collaboration in securities market regulation and development, as well as further deepening mutual market access between the Mainland and Hong Kong.

In the afternoon meeting with Assistant Minister of Commerce Yuan Xiaoming, Mr Chan discussed with Mr Yuan the further deepening of economic and trade co-operation.

Secretary for Commerce & Economic Development Algernon Yau, who joined the meeting, signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Director-General of the MOC’s Department of Taiwan, Hong Kong & Macao Affairs Sun Yi.

Mr Yau also signed another MOU with Director-General of the MOC’s Department of Pilot Free Trade Zone & Free Trade Port He Yongqian.

The two MOUs were signed in accordance with the mechanism of the Mainland & Hong Kong Economic & Trade Co-operation Committee. Mr Chan and Mr Yuan witnessed the ceremony.

Through the signing of these MOUs, the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government and the MOC will further strengthen exchanges and co-operation between the Mainland and Hong Kong in key economic and trade areas, and deepen the alignment of Mainland's pilot free trade zones and free trade port with Hong Kong, respectively.

The MOUs also serve to fully leverage the respective advantages of the two places, jointly serving the country’s high-level opening-up, as well as bringing economic and trade co-operation between the Mainland and Hong Kong to new heights.

Mr Chan thanked the MOC for its continuous strong support for the Hong Kong SAR Government’s efforts to promote Hong Kong’s economic and trade development.

Mr Chan said the Hong Kong SAR Government will leverage the advantages of Hong Kong’s internationalised business environment, professional services system and global resources network, to further give full play to the city’s dual roles as a “super connector" and a ‘super value-adder”.

The Hong Kong SAR Government will also enhance the city’s competitiveness and international influence, consolidate its status as an international trade centre, while contributing to the country’s high-quality economic development, he added.

In the afternoon, Mr Chan also visited an artificial intelligence company and met its senior management.
